name: Hallucination and Grounding
intent: Understand why a language model can state false things fluently and confidently, and how grounding in sources, abstaining and checking reduce the risk.
scenario: A research assistant cites a court case that does not exist. The name, the court and the date all look right, and the summary reads well. Nobody checks it until a lawyer tries to find the case.
problem: A language model is trained to produce text that is a likely continuation of its input. It is not looking facts up, and nothing in the basic mechanism marks a statement as unknown. When it lacks the fact, or the fact is rare or conflicting in its training data, the most likely continuation can still be a fluent and wrong one. The reader sees the same confident tone either way, so errors are hard to spot without a check.

howItWorks.title: The model predicts plausible text
howItWorks.text: At each step the model chooses a likely next token given everything so far. A date, a name or a citation is a string that fits the pattern of the text. If the true fact is not available to the model, a plausible-looking one fits the pattern just as well.

howItWorks.title: Where wrong answers come from
howItWorks.text: Facts can be missing from the training data, rare, out of date or contradicted by other text. A question can contain a false premise that the model goes along with. And a model tuned to be helpful may prefer to give an answer over saying that it does not know. The survey by Ji and colleagues defines hallucination as generated content that is nonsensical or unfaithful to the provided source.

howItWorks.title: Lower temperature is not a cure
howItWorks.text: Temperature controls how random the choice is, not how much the model knows. At a low temperature the model repeats its most likely answer, and if that answer is wrong it is wrong nearly every time.

howItWorks.title: Grounding: give it the sources
howItWorks.text: Retrieval-augmented generation finds relevant passages and gives them to the model with the question, asking for an answer based on them. The RAG paper, which trained a retriever and a generator together, presented retrieval as a non-parametric memory that can be swapped to update its knowledge, and to improve factual output. The answer should cite the passages it used.

howItWorks.title: Abstain when there is no support
howItWorks.text: A grounded system should be able to say 'I could not find this in the documents'. That means giving the model permission and a clear instruction to decline, and testing that it does so when the sources do not contain the answer. An instruction helps but is not a guarantee.

howItWorks.title: Check the claims, and measure the rate
howItWorks.text: A separate step can test whether each claim in an answer is supported by the cited passage, with a checking model, rules or a human. For high-stakes uses a person reviews the result. To know how bad the problem is, score a set of questions with known answers and track the share of unsupported claims over time.

pros: Grounding ties answers to documents the user can open and check
Updating the documents updates the answers, without retraining the model
Abstaining turns some confident errors into an honest 'not found'
A claim checker catches many unsupported statements before the user sees them
cons: Retrieval can miss the right passage, and the model may still invent an answer
A model can cite a passage that does not actually support its claim
Abstaining too readily makes the assistant unhelpful
Checking adds latency and cost, and a checker can be wrong as well
whenToUse: Answers must be traceable to documents, as in legal, medical, financial or support use
The facts change often or are private to your organisation
You need a measure of how often the assistant says things its sources do not support
whenNotToUse: Do not expect a prompt that says 'do not make things up' to stop it on its own
Do not treat a fluent, detailed answer as evidence that it is correct
Do not skip human review for decisions where a wrong answer causes real harm
pitfalls: Trusting citations without checking that the cited passage says what the answer claims
Measuring only on questions whose answers are in the documents, and never on ones that are not
Lowering the temperature and treating the problem as solved
Fixing one visible wrong answer by editing the prompt, without testing for new ones

roles.label: Question
roles.description: What the user asks. It may not be answerable from the sources at all.

roles.label: Model
roles.description: Writes a fluent answer. On its own it has no way to mark what it does not know.

roles.label: Sources
roles.description: Retrieved passages that the answer should rest on and cite.

roles.label: Checker
roles.description: Tests whether each claim is supported by a source, and lets the system abstain or flag the rest.

quiz.question: A research assistant cites a court case that does not exist, with a plausible name, court and date. Which statement best explains how this happens?
options: The model looked up a database of cases, and the database contained a corrupted entry
The model deliberately invents details whenever the user's question is difficult to answer
The model generates text that fits the pattern of a citation, and without grounding it has no check that the case is real
The model's temperature was too low, which forces it to repeat the same invented case
quiz.explanation: A model produces likely text, and a citation is a pattern with a name, a court and a date. If the real case is not in front of it, a plausible-looking one fits the pattern. It does not look anything up or deliberately lie, and a low temperature does not create the case.

quiz.question: A team sets the temperature to 0 to remove hallucinations, but the assistant still gives the same wrong answer to a question every time. Why?
options: Temperature controls randomness, not knowledge, so a wrong top answer is repeated consistently
A temperature of 0 makes the model skip its knowledge and answer from the prompt alone
The wrong answer is stored in the model's cache, and it must be cleared by the provider
The question was too long, and long questions always produce wrong answers at low temperature
quiz.explanation: A low temperature removes variation, so the model gives its most likely answer each time. If that answer is wrong, the error becomes reliable. Reducing hallucination needs grounding, abstaining or checking, not a lower temperature.

quiz.question: A retrieval-based assistant sometimes states things that are not in the passages it retrieved. Which addition is most likely to reduce this?
options: Retrieve more passages, so that the model always has more text to quote from
Increase the model's temperature, so that it explores answers that match the passages better
Remove the citations from the answer, because citations only encourage invented details
Require each claim to cite a passage, check the claims against the passages, and abstain when none supports them
quiz.explanation: Checking each claim against its cited passage catches statements that the sources do not support, and abstaining handles the case where nothing supports an answer. More passages can add noise, a higher temperature adds randomness, and removing citations removes the means to verify.
